body:
In the 6.3 text we say:

> This section contains general requirements for the security of authentication mechanisms as well as setting out the different expectations for levels including requiring multi-factor for L2 and supporting hardware-based mechanisms for L3, such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance.

All of the larger IDPs supports hardware-based authentication mechanisms. Simply supporting hardware-based authentication mechanisms does not mean that the users of such authentication systems are more secure. I therefor see little reason why you should make a point of it for L3 unless you **require** the use of hardware-based authentication, that is, unless a clear plan accompanied an exception on how the risks around authentication will be mitigated, taking into account NIST's guidance and research on the topic.. I would rather see that ASVS 5  Level 3 aligned with AAL3 in this regard. 

Please see comment from @tghosth https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2925#issuecomment-2792342067

> Clarify in the requirement whether single-factor hardware-based auth is sufficient for L3 or whether multi-factor is still required

Please read: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3-Implementation-Resources/63B/AAL/

> Although two authentication factors are required at AAL3, one combination of authenticators (Hardware Single-Factor OTP Device plus a Single-Factor Cryptographic Software Authenticator plus a Memorized Secret) consists of three authenticators. This combination stems from the fact that the hardware-based Single-Factor OTP Devices do not provide verifier impersonation resistance, so a Single-Factor Cryptographic Software Authenticator can satisfy that requirement. But since both of those authenticators are something you have, a Memorized Secret is required to satisfy the requirement for two different authentication factors.

This clarifies the need to require MFA for Level 3, but it goes beyond that listing, specifically the 3 requirement necessary to satisfy AAL3.

In addition to all requirements inherent to AAL2, the following requirements apply to AAL3, to my understanding:

- The use of authenticators must guarantee impersonation resistance
- The use of authenticators must guarantee compromise resistance
- The use of authenticators must guarantee authentication intent

In the interest of aligning ASVS with NIST, it seems reasonable to ensure that these 3 requirements are needed in order to ensure that an application satisfy ASVS Level 3.

This is consistent with NIST SP800 63b, 2.3.1: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/aal/#aal3 

> AAL3 authentication SHALL require one of the following authenticator combinations:
> 
> - Multi-factor cryptographic authentication ([Sec. 3.1.7](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#mfc))
> - Single-factor cryptographic authentication ([Sec. 3.1.6](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#sfc)) used in conjunction with a password ([Sec. 3.1.1](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#password))

Based on the 3 requirements inherent to AAL3 it is still possible to ask for a waver given that the first 3 requirements are meet if there are compensating controls that guarantees these three. So the following could be added:

_Verify that security decisions based on threat analysis is documented in situations where multi-factor or hardware-based authentication not is achievable or realistic, and that compensating controls that achieve the underlying three formal authenticator assurances (impersonation-, compromise resistance and authentication intent) have been deployed._


Given all of this, the text under V6.3 should be changed from:

**V6.3 General Authentication Security**
This section contains general requirements for the security of authentication mechanisms as well as setting out the different expectations for levels including requiring multi-factor for L2 and supporting hardware-based mechanisms for L3, such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance.

to:

**V6.3 General Authentication Security**
This section contains general requirements for the security of authentication mechanisms and sets out the different expectations for levels. In particular, enforcing the use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required for L2, and requiring hardware-based mechanisms (such as standards provided by the Fast IDentity Online (FIDO) Alliance) is required for L3.

Whilst this is a relatively aggressive stance on MFA, it is critical to raise the bar to protect users. Any attempt to relax these requirements should be accompanied by a clear plan for mitigating the risks around authentication, taking into account NIST's guidance and research on the topic.

Note that at the time of release, NIST SP 800-63 considers email as [not acceptable](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b11) as an authentication mechanism ([archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20250330115328/https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b11)).

The requirements in this section relate to a variety of sections of [NIST's Guidance](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html), including: [§ 4.2.1](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#421-permitted-authenticator-types), [§ 4.3.1](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#431-permitted-authenticator-types), [§ 5.2.2](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#522-rate-limiting-throttling), and [§ 6.1.2](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#-612-post-enrollment-binding).

and...

6.3.2 | Verify that the application requires users to either use a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms. | 2
-- | -- | --| 

to:

6.3.2 | Verify that the application requires users to either use a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms (e.g. cryptographic authentication in conjunction with a password). | 2
-- | -- | --| 

The following Level 3 requirement need to be changed from:

6.3.7 | Verify that a hardware-based authentication mechanism is supported that provides impersonation resistance against phishing attacks (such as WebAuthn) and verifies intent to authenticate by requiring a user-initiated action (such as a button press on a FIDO hardware key). | 3
-- | -- | --

To:

6.3.7 | Verify that a hardware-based authentication mechanism that provides compromise- and impersonation resistance (e.g: against phishing attacks), through the use of authentication standards (such as WebAuthn), is required, and that it verifies intent to authenticate by requiring a user-initiated action (such as a button press on a FIDO hardware key). | 3
-- | -- | --


We could preferably refer to «confidential computing» instead of «hardware-based» as the latter could be misunderstood, given that most Intel and AMD chips now come with a TEE or TPM.

«Confidential Computing is the protection of data in use by performing computation in a hardware-based, attested Trusted Execution Environment."», see definition under 2.1: https://confidentialcomputing.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/10/2023/03/CCC-A-Technical-Analysis-of-Confidential-Computing-v1.3_unlocked.pdf

Also, for reference:

Intel DAL:https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/dal/technical-details.html
AMD: https://docs.amd.com/r/en-US/wp548-single-chip-fips/Introduction-to-Secure-Execution-Environment
Android: https://source.android.com/docs/security/features/trusty 
IPhone: https://support.apple.com/guide/security/secure-enclave-sec59b0b31ff/web

Please note that I am stating that hardware-based authentication should be **required**, not just supported. This is very much achievable and should be the case as it is one of the few possibilities  we know of that digitally will satisfy the underlying requirements of compromise- and impersonation resistance together with verifying whether the action is user-initiated. The later can be achieved by inspecting the UV flag (https://w3c.github.io/webauthn/#abstract-opdef-credential-record-uvinitialized), the former by looking at the ACR and AMR claims. 

For reference regarding "compensating controls", please read: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-8 

So as an alternative, instead of the following:

Verify that security decisions based on threat analysis is documented in situations where multi-factor or hardware-based authentication not is achievable or realistic, and that compensating controls that achieve the underlying three formal authenticator assurances (impersonation-, compromise resistance and authentication intent) have been deployed.

 we could instead simplify this as:

_Verify, in situations where authentication requirements not is achievable or realistic, by demonstrating comparability of any chosen alternative, to include any compensating controls, when the complete set of applicable requirements not is implemented._

se also my response: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2925#issuecomment-2805269821 

So My suggestion is that we add the following under V15


15.2.5 | Verify, in situations where application security requirements not is achievable or realistic, by demonstrating comparability of any chosen alternative, to include any compensating controls, when the complete set of applicable requirements not is implemented. | 2
-- | -- | --

Ok, firstly apologies for the delay in response @sydseter .

I have read through all of this and have a few initial thoughts:

1) Requiring some form of MFA for L2 was controversial but I think achievable and justifiable. However, I think that requiring hardware MFA for L3 is not. I am thinking about consumer facing banking and medical apps.
2) I think the 15.2.5 concept is a little too generic for a usable requirement. I think we need to make exceptions rarely and otherwise rely on the catch-all comply or explain approach for ASVS.
3) I can see that there is some subtlety in hardware based authentication but I really don't want to get bogged down in all the details and I don't think it provides a benefit for developers or security.
4) I don't think we should assume that L1-3 of ASVS exactly matches to AAL1-AAL3 of NIST.
5) I think that if we are requiring MFA then we are requiring MFA and that means two different authentication factors. For example, passkeys generally require that you have access to a private key (something you have) and then you access the certificate by either pass phrase/PIN/pattern (something you know) or a fingerprint (something you are).
6) I think that as it is, this requirement 6.3.7 covers the goal of impersonation resistance well whilst also putting the onus on the user to take advantage of it.

I think that we can clarify in this requirement that this is not requiring enforcement but rather just support and then I don't think I would do anything else.

In Europe, consumer-facing banking and medical apps are required to follow AAL3. In those cases, ASVS is irrelevant. Are you referring to other parts of the world? I strongly disagree with this. Access to banking and medical data should require using AAL3, no matter where you are. There have been numerous cases in recent years where medical and banking data have been stolen because of relaxed authentication requirements. The consequences for the consumers have been severe. 

Last year NIST came with some clarifications regarding AAL2 and AAL3: https://fidoalliance.org/nist-cites-phishing-resistance-of-synced-passkeys-in-digital-identity-guidelines-update/

**Synced Passkeys** has been recognized for their [phishing resistance](https://www.corbado.com/blog/passkeys-phishing-resistant), and synced passkeys therefore meet AAL2 requirements by ensuring secure and encrypted transmission of authentication data.
**Device-Bound Passkeys** is said to meet AAL3 standards due to their hardware-based authentication, providing very high confidence in the control of authenticators. 

Device-Bound passkeys are supported by the following systems:

- Windows 10 (EOL: October 14, 2025) and newer. 
- macOS Ventura (EOL: November 30, 2025) and newer.
- ChromeOS 109 (EOL: October 10, 2023 ) and newer.
- iOS 16 (EOL: 18 Sep 2023) and newer.
- Android 9 (EOL: 01 Jan 2022) and newer. 

https://passkeys.dev/device-support/#advanced

This is why I believe it is no longer an issue to require the use of Device-Bound (hardware-based) passkeys for ASVS Level 3.

> In Europe, consumer-facing banking and medical apps are required to follow AAL3

I appreciate that UK is not exactly Europe but I access a UK bank account without cryptographic authentication.

> Passkeys

Passkeys almost always have some sort of fall back such as magic link which eliminates their phishing resistance.  They currently also have terrible UX. I would not want to mandate them for those two reasons.

> I appreciate that UK is not exactly Europe but I access a UK bank account without cryptographic authentication.

FWIW, I access a bank account in EU without cryptographic authentication. 😄

> In Europe, consumer-facing banking and medical apps are required to follow AAL3.

I checked just at the moment and I did access French [Mon Espace Santé](https://www.monespacesante.fr/) (official centralized state-provided patient healthcare record) without any cryptographic authentication. 😄

Last time I checked many other French patient healthcare websites did not require cryptographic authentication for patients either.
I agree that L3 apps (or NIST 800-83b AAL3 apps) should require smart cards, hardware tokens or other cryptographic exchange. Mobile apps in certain phones solve this purpose.

You are right, I am wrong.

The European Banking Regulation require [Strong Customer Authentication (SCA)](https://finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/strong-customer-authentication-requirement-psd2-comes-force_en)

This means 2 out of the following 3:

- somthing you have
- something you know
- something the user is

But, yes, that does not mean device-bound authentication is used.

Still, in practice, that is what is being used.

Regarding access to health data. Device-bound authentication has probably not been adopted by all country, but once eIDAS has been rolled out, it is going to be a requirement to use eIDAS to access health data in Europe. https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4dd47ec2-71dd-49fc-b036-ad7c14f6ed68_en?filename=ehealth_ehds_qa_en.pdf

> IDAS has been rolled out, it is going to be a requirement to use eIDAS to access health data in Europe.

https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-standards-and-technical-specifications/blob/main/docs/technical-specifications/README.md

Looks like the technical specifications are at a very early stage and there is no guarantee they will require a hardware authenticator is there?

> AAL3

I repeat that we don't necessarily want to map L3 to AAL3 but having looked at this more carefully, I think there are two different things we are talking about here:

1) Cryptographic authenticator (some sort of stored key)
2) Hardware authenticator (dedicated hardware device or enclave used to protect a cryptographic key.

AAL3 talks about a cryptographic authenticator, it talks about hardware as details but doesn't specifically mandate anything.

In any case, I think it is irrelevant, both mechanisms are very hard to get non tech savvy people to use and the recovery flows are even more painful. Expecting that all banking apps will start requiring all users to use these mechanisms is pie in the sky and right now it is not clear to me how many banks even support their use. **To me, the latter would be a better fight right now and that is what I really want to push.**

When we talk about a hardware-based cryptographic authenticator, we refer to devices that have an integrated circuit isolated from the main processor, which is meant for cryptographic operations and is commonly named a secure hardware module. Most mobile devices and laptops have built-in support for this, and all major operating systems support it. Yes, it can also be a separate hardware key, but it does not have to be, and in most cases it is not.
Today, if a device supports passkeys, it also comes with an integrated isolated circuit for such purposes.
On Apple devices, this is called "Secure Enclave", on Windows it is called "Trusted Platform Module" (TPM), and on Android, "Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)".

The number of online accounts that can leverage passkeys today is said to be around 15 billion and rising: https://fidoalliance.org/passkey-adoption-doubles-in-2024-more-than-15-billion-online-accounts-can-leverage-passkeys/

To get users to use this is not far-fetched; it is happening at a breathtaking pace.

When NIST refers to passkeys, they distinguish between passkeys that are synced and passkeys that aren't synced. That distinction will probably not last, but hardware-based cryptographic authentication is still widely supported. 

If the sentiment is that hardware-based authentication should still only be supported for ASVS Level 3, then we should probably clarify the use of the word "hardware-based" whether we refer to [device-bound (residential) passkey authentication](https://www.passkeycentral.org/introduction-to-passkeys/passkey-types#device-bound-passkeys), [synced passkeys](https://www.passkeycentral.org/introduction-to-passkeys/passkey-types#synced-passkeys), or both.

After reviewing issue #2970 regarding MFA requirements for Level 3, I'd like to contribute to the discussion about whether hardware-based authentication should be "supported" or "required" at this level.

### Analysis of Current Wording

The current wording in section 6.3 and requirement 6.3.8 uses "supporting hardware-based mechanisms for L3" and "Verify that a hardware-based authentication mechanism is supported..." This creates ambiguity about whether hardware-based authentication is mandatory for all users at Level 3 or merely needs to be available as an option.

### Alignment with NIST SP 800-63

NIST SP 800-63 AAL3 explicitly requires hardware-based authenticators for all authentication events, not just as an available option. The standard states:

"AAL3 authentication requires the use of a hardware-based authenticator that provides phishing resistance."

The key requirements for AAL3 include:
1. Impersonation resistance
2. Compromise resistance
3. Authentication intent

These are achieved through hardware-based authenticators or specific combinations of authenticators that together provide these properties.

### Security Implications

There's a significant security difference between supporting hardware-based authentication (making it available as an option) and requiring it (mandating its use for all users). Simply supporting hardware authenticators without requiring them creates a potential security gap - users can choose less secure authentication methods, undermining the security posture intended for Level 3 applications.

### Recommendation

I support the proposed changes to requirement 6.3.8:

"Verify that a hardware-based authentication mechanism that provides compromise- and impersonation resistance (e.g., against phishing attacks), through the use of authentication standards (such as WebAuthn), is required, and that it verifies intent to authenticate by requiring a user-initiated action (such as a button press on a FIDO hardware key)."

This change would:
1. Align ASVS Level 3 more closely with NIST AAL3
2. Eliminate ambiguity about whether hardware-based authentication is optional or mandatory
3. Ensure that applications claiming Level 3 compliance truly provide the high level of authentication security appropriate for highly sensitive applications

### Compensating Controls

I also support the suggestion to add language about compensating controls for situations where hardware-based authentication might not be feasible, provided that the three core properties (impersonation resistance, compromise resistance, and authentication intent) are still achieved through other means:

"Verify that security decisions based on threat analysis is documented in situations where multi-factor or hardware-based authentication is not achievable or realistic, and that compensating controls that achieve the underlying three formal authenticator assurances (impersonation resistance, compromise resistance, and authentication intent) have been deployed."

This provides flexibility while maintaining the security principles that underpin AAL3.

Those arguments here are nice and logical, but I share the same concern as Josh [pointed out](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2970#issuecomment-2841352555) - if the context is some internal web application, or with a controlled user-base, then we can _require_ it. If it is a worldwide accessible service to be used for everyone and from everywhere, I think it is not realistic to require it?

For example, do we consider Gmail to be a level 3 application?

Thank you for raising this important practical consideration. You've highlighted a key challenge in implementing strict hardware-based authentication requirements for globally accessible applications.

### Clarifying ASVS Level 3 Scope

ASVS Level 3 is specifically designed for high-value, high-assurance, or high-safety applications - typically those in sectors like military, healthcare, critical infrastructure, or financial systems handling large transactions. These are applications where the security requirements justifiably outweigh some convenience factors.

Public-facing services like Gmail would likely target ASVS Level 2 compliance rather than Level 3, as Level 3 imposes controls that may be impractical for mass consumer applications. Level 3 is intended for applications where the risk profile justifies stricter controls.

### The Value of Compensating Controls

This is precisely why I suggested including language about compensating controls in the requirement. For applications that legitimately need Level 3 security but face practical constraints in implementing hardware-based authentication for all users, the standard should allow for well-documented alternatives that still achieve the three core security properties:

1. Impersonation resistance
2. Compromise resistance
3. Authentication intent

### Proposed Approach

I believe we can address this concern by:

1. Maintaining the stronger "required" language to align with NIST AAL3
2. Explicitly acknowledging that compensating controls are acceptable when:
   - The application has documented why hardware-based authentication isn't feasible
   - Alternative controls are implemented that achieve equivalent security properties
   - The decision is based on a formal threat analysis

This approach maintains the security intent of Level 3 while providing flexibility for real-world implementation challenges.

### Regarding Gmail

To directly address your question: Gmail would likely not be classified as requiring Level 3 compliance under ASVS. However, for high-security Gmail users (government officials, executives, journalists in dangerous regions), Google does offer their Advanced Protection Program which requires hardware security keys - effectively implementing Level 3 controls for their highest-risk users while maintaining Level 2 controls for the general user base.

This tiered approach might be a model worth considering - requiring hardware-based authentication for the highest-risk users or most sensitive functions within an application, while allowing alternative strong authentication methods for other users.

The compensating controls I mentioned are meant to provide flexibility in implementation while still maintaining the security principles, not to create loopholes that undermine the standard.

But you can certainly configure gmail for _organizations_ to **_require_** hardware authentication for L3 organizations. Like many identity providers, the AuthN strength and requirements are configurable per-organization. So you certainly can make gmail for organizations L3 if you want to.
ping @danielcuthbert - is hardware-based authN must have for consumers for bank systems? And is it realistic? Taking into account the time window for the next, let's say 4 years?

@elarlang To answer that we need to agree on what «hardware-based» is. I would say yes, because, to me, «hardware-based» is found in every device that has an integrated circuit isolated from the main processor meant for cryptography. That is found in every Android, Iphone and Laptop on sale out there right now. And about 18 billion accounts and every major operative system supports it. 

If a bank isn’t able to give the consumer that possibility, then it’s just because they are too greedy or lazy to do so.

I value this discussion. To clarify: while flexibility in implementation is important, we cannot compromise on the security standards that define L3.

The core principles - resistance to impersonation, compromise, and clear authentication intent - must remain non-negotiable as already mentioned in my previous comments. Organizations can adapt their methods, but the outcome should never change.

As @sydseter rightly pointed out, hardware-based authentication is now widespread. For L3-level applications, it’s not just reasonable, it’s essential to preserve L3’s integrity.

Flexibility in execution is fine. Compromise on security is not.

Yes, and, in many ways the expression «hardware-based» belongs to another time before FIDO implementations became widespread. It will not age well. Alternatively we could drop the expression altogether. Every phone provider is gunning for having «synced passkeys» without attestation being the default. We could debate whether it is more appropriate to mandate «device-bound» passkeys for L3, but I would let that be up to whoever is doing the implementation. In the interest of simplicity and future proofing it would perhaps be better to talk about what can be considered «core principles» as @anonymous-31 points out.

#### Clarifying Question(s)

1) In this example, are the participants in the "healthcare" and "financial systems handling large transactions" sectors* assumed to be part of a "controlled user-base"?  

2) For this example, is it important if they are or are-not? 
 



#### Disclaimer

\* = ex: healthcare professionals vs patients. (Presumably the military and critical infrastructure sectors are implicitly controlled user-bases)

Those are valid questions, and it is pretty much the thing that I try to figure out here myself (starting from https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2970#issuecomment-2844274971).

In the beginning, I associated "hardware-based" MFA more like a requirement to hand out yubikeys to the user base, and in this context, the question is valid to ask. But putting more time into the topic, I understand that a lot of current auth solutions actually satisfy the NIST AAL3 level.

Ok, I think there are four options for our default position here, three of which are problematic.

1) We require an L3 app to enforce hardware based authentication which means no synced passkeys and no fallback options. For large consumer facing apps, I don't see a realistic way to handle this at scale because there are no good recovery options and the app owner would spend their entire time helping people recover their accounts. I don't think this is feasible.

2) We require  an L3 app to enforce cryptographic authentication without requiring hardware and therefore allowing synced passkeys but we **do not** allow fallback options. This takes us out of line with AAL3, is less secure but still has a similar level of pain from an account recovery perspective. I don't think this is feasible either.

3) We require an L3 app to enforce cryptographic authentication without requiring hardware and therefore allowing synced passkeys but we **do** allow fallback options (magic links, etc). We are now requiring extra functionality that doesn't actually provide any major security uplift. I don't see the point in this.

4) We require an L3 app to **support** hardware-based authenticators (or some variant). We therefore give users the option to better secure their accounts without the issues in the previous 3 options. We aren't aligned with AAL3 but I don't think that is a critical goal.


> The core principles - resistance to impersonation, compromise, and clear authentication intent - must remain non-negotiable 

@anonymous-31

The part under negotiation is whether this must be enforced for all users or just supported for all users. My arguments above are that enforcing for all users is unrealistic but we should absolutely be mandating that L3 apps provide support for this ability to give users the ability to improve their security. I already think this would be a major uplift.

> If a bank isn’t able to give the consumer that possibility, then it’s just because they are too greedy or lazy to do so.

@sydseter

Key word here is possibility, I am advocating that they provide the possibility. My understanding is that you are going further and saying they have to force it on consumers.


Questions for anyone who wishes to respond:

1) Are synced passkeys an acceptable solution?
2) How do you handle the massive customer support burden of:
  a) Forcing all users onto passkeys without fallback options, bearing in mind that not all consumers of L3 apps are techies with new smartphones and laptops.
  b) Handling constant account recovery issues for these users.
3) If you are advocating for passkeys with fallback options, what is the security benefit of that?a


Overall, I think that people have lost sight of "[AviD's Rule of Usability](https://security.stackexchange.com/a/6116)":

> Security at the expense of usability comes at the expense of security.

Keep in mind that AAL3/NIST 800-63b which loosely maps to L3 ASVS is reserved for critical infrastructure and not consumer apps.

Think apps that shoot missles, or health care apps that order controlled substances at scale, or apps that manage billions of private records, or access to classified systems, or control of critical infrastructure for large companies (like a root level AWS account).

I would not consider consumer banking or consumer health care and similar to be L3.

In the context of mapping L3 closer to NIST 800-63b AAL3, then hardware AuthN is very sensible and has been a part of digital identity standards for over 5 years.

> Keep in mind that AAL3/NIST 800-63b which loosely maps to L3 ASVS is reserved for critical infrastructure **and not consumer apps**.

Can we have facts and quotes for this?

> Think apps that shoot missles, or health care apps that order controlled substances at scale, or apps that manage billions of private records, or access to classified systems, or control of critical infrastructure for large companies (like a root level AWS account).

This is a serious niche. I also think those are not in mass, having their own specific requirements and are per their own niche with their own specific needs. It means they don't need ASVS that much.

> I would not consider consumer banking or consumer health care and similar to be L3.

Based on my comments above, strong disagreement here with that.

We should take consumer banking and consumer healthcare as starter for L3.

> For large consumer facing apps, I don't see a realistic way to handle this at scale because there are no good recovery options and the app owner would spend their entire time helping people recover their accounts. I don't think this is feasible.

I think you need to keep in mind that, in the cases where L3 is requiered, the question of recovery will need to be thought through from the moment the customer is onboarded. I can think of muliple ways both support and customer services could ensure a smooth transition from a usability and recovery perspective and still keep a thight grip on customer satisfaction while ensuring the L3 principles are followed at the level of security required.

Still, to me it doesn’t seem appropriate to solve 
the recovery and support challenges when we need to decide which authentication level is appropriate. Those are important, but still separate concerns that should be discussed once we have agreed on what is the appropriate authentication level we need to have for L3. This is a **fascinating** issue to me, especially given my current obsession with trying to get modern auth systems designed and used by all. First, I believe it’s important to reinforce that Level 3 has always served as the aspirational model of what a secure application should look like. It’s the Lamborghini on the bedroom wall, perhaps elusive for many, but no less worth striving for. 

With that in mind, I support the position that hardware-based authentication should be required, not merely supported, at ASVS Level 3. This level should represent the pinnacle of application security maturity, and the mandatory use of phishing-resistant, hardware-based authenticators such as FIDO2/U2F tokens should be part of that definition. 

Ideally, we want this standard to encourage the use of hardware-based authentication mechanisms, such as FIDO2/U2F tokens, as a baseline requirement for high assurance systems. 

Given the current crop of attacks and adversaries that abuse authentication flows, hardware-backed authenticators do provide substantial resilience against such attacks and this aligns the standard of achieving parity with NIST's 800-63B AAL3

That said, I also acknowledge the operational and implementation challenges that mandatory hardware tokens may pose. Therefore, the language of the requirement should carefully distinguish between:

- Support: The applications technical capability to integrate with hardware-based authenticators, and 
- Require: A policy-driven enforcement that mandates the use of hardware-based authenticators for all users of L3 applications

This is making things more complicated than they need to be.

First of all, there is a clear consensus, among us, and around the globe, that AAL3, IAL3, FAL3, and eIDAS LoA3 are **required** when doing business transactions that can be considered high-risk.. This is not only relevant to banking and health, but also to sectors like pharmaceutical, insurance, property, governmental services, critical infrastructure, and various other cross-border transactions.

Device-bound passkeys are the only technical authentication equivalent that can give this level of assurance. Synced passkeys can be both software-based and hardware-based. Synced passkeys do not appropriately prove ownership or intent because they lack attestation. This is not an issue for L2, but for L3 it is, legally speaking.  

Some things to consider:

- MFA and hardware-based authentication are additive, not supplementary.
- FIDO2/U2F tokens can be software-based and stored in a password manager, but that does not give any high assurance needed for what is being considered above from a risk perspective.
- When FIDO2/U2F tokens are backed up, they lose their attestation. For high assurance, believe it or not, backup is not allowed. I know this doesn't seem easy, but the entire population of the European Union seems to do just fine despite it. 

So for ASVS L3 authenticators, the following requirement should hold:

1. The authenticator must be device-bound.
2. The authenticator must require multi-factor.
3. The authenticator can not be backed up.
4. The authentication must be performed in an attested and trusted execution environment (TEE) or by authenticators with AAL3 assurance or equivalent.

"or equivalent" is important because each European member nation is implementing their eIDAS LoA3 authenticator that is not necessarily based on FIDO2 or WebAuthN
